Course: Information Security (week 7, topic: password storage, status: KNOWN).

Question: We were asked about password storage in Information Security. Say what password storage means in practice and why it matters. Mark my answer against the official points, please.

Student answer: MD5 is fine here because it is one-way. Hash the password twice and keep the database private and nobody can get the passwords back. I am not sure about the rest of it.

Official rubric points:
1. Says a general-purpose hash is unsuitable because it is fast
2. Names a per-user salt and says what it defeats
3. Names a deliberately slow password hash
4. Says the work factor is tuned and raised over time

Verdict: incorrect - 0 of 4 points, though the answer is a common and understandable one.

Not earned: all 4 points. Your answer says "MD5 is fine here because it is one-way. Hash the password twice and keep the database private and nobody can get the passwords back. I am not sure about the rest of it." - and none of the rubric points can be read into that.

The idea that needs replacing: that a password hash is judged by how unbreakable the algorithm sounds, when the property that matters is how slow it is per guess.
The correct statement: Replace the fast hash with bcrypt or Argon2 at a tuned cost factor, and give every account its own random salt.
The mechanism: An attacker who steals the table guesses offline, so your only lever is the time each guess costs: a fast hash gives them billions per second, a tuned bcrypt gives them a few thousand.

To prove the fix stuck: Take your current code, swap the hash for bcrypt with a cost factor you time on your own machine, and write down how many guesses per second that cost buys the attacker.

Pigeonhole settles it: more possible keys than buckets means collisions are guaranteed, so a hash function is judged on uniformity, not on avoidance. What keeps lookups near O(1) is the pairing of a good spread with a bounded load factor and a resize-and-rehash policy. Worst case stays O(n) - which is why libraries randomise seeds, to stop an attacker crafting keys that all land in one bucket.

That instinct about hash table collisions is the common one, and it is worth naming rather than just correcting: that a good hash function makes collisions go away, rather than making them rare and evenly spread.

Treat collisions as certain and design for their distribution: pick a resolution strategy, watch the load factor, and rehash before buckets get long. The key space is unbounded and the table is not, so the only question a hash function settles is how evenly the unavoidable collisions are spread.

Test it yourself rather than taking my word for it: Insert 1,000 keys that deliberately share a bucket in your implementation and measure lookup time against 1,000 well-spread keys.

Course: Computer Networks (week 2, topic: bandwidth versus latency, status: KNOWN).

Question: I answered this in the Computer Networks quiz and got it back with no comments. Explain bandwidth versus latency and say what actually decides the outcome. What would a marker say?

Student answer: Reducing the number of requests made the page faster, so HTTP requests are expensive to parse.

Official rubric points:
1. Defines bandwidth as throughput per unit time
2. Defines latency as one-way or round-trip delay
3. Says more bandwidth does not reduce round-trip time
4. Identifies a latency-bound workload

Verdict: partially_correct (1/4). The gap is specific and fixable.

Credit where it is due: the conclusion is the one I would reach. "Reducing the number of requests made the page faster, so HTTP requests are expensive to parse." lands on the right action.
Not earned: the justification is what the rubric is marking, and yours does not hold - the fix worked, but the cost removed was round trips, not parsing.

What is actually going wrong: that a faster connection means a lower delay, because both are reported to users as speed.
Replace it with this: Measure which one binds first: count the round trips your page needs and multiply by the round-trip time before buying capacity.
Why: Bandwidth widens the pipe but the propagation and queueing delay of each round trip is unchanged, so a page made of 60 dependent small requests is limited by 60 times the round-trip time.

Do this next: Load your project page with the network panel open, record the round-trip time and the number of requests, and compute how much of the load time is unavoidable at the current latency.

Bandwidth and latency are independent. Bandwidth is bits per second - it decides how long a large transfer takes. Latency is the delay of a single trip, set mostly by distance, queueing and processing, and it does not improve when the pipe widens. A page with many dependent small requests is latency-bound: its floor is the number of sequential round trips times the round-trip time. Official rubric points:

Java is gaslighting me. I'm comparing strings with `==` like I always have in Python. Sometimes it works! `String a = "go"; String b = "go"; a == b` is true — I tested it! But the same comparison on a string the user typed in comes back false even when I can PRINT both strings and see they're identical. Same operator, same-looking strings, different results. How is this not a bug in Java?

The cruelest part of your situation is the 'sometimes it works' — if `==` failed every time, you'd have fixed this in five minutes. So let's explain both halves: why it fails, and — the half that actually matters — why it ever succeeded.

First half. In Java, a `String` variable doesn't hold the text; it holds a *reference* — an arrow pointing at a String object in memory. So spell out what question `a == b` is actually asking in Java. Is it about the text?

If they're arrows, then `==` compares the arrows — 'do these point at the SAME object?' — not the letters. Two separate String objects could both contain 'go' and `==` would say false because they're two boxes at two addresses. Fine, that explains the user-input failure. But then my test should ALSO have failed! `a` and `b` were two separate variables — why did `==` say true for my two literals?

That's the right question, and its answer is the trap's engine. When the compiler sees the *literal* "go" written twice in your source code, it plays a memory-saving trick called **interning**: identical compile-time literals are folded into ONE shared object in a string pool. So `a` and `b` are two arrows pointing at the same pooled object — `==` honestly answers 'same object? yes.' Your test accidentally asked the one question where arrow-equality and text-equality coincide.

User input, file reads, string concatenation at runtime — those build *fresh* objects at runtime; the pool trick doesn't apply. Now diagnose yourself like a doctor would: which Python fact did you import as if it were universal, and what made Python safe for that habit?

Java is gaslighting me. I'm comparing strings with `==` like I always have in Python. Sometimes it works! `String a = "go"; String b = "go"; a == b` is true — I tested it! But the same comparison on a string the user typed in comes back false even when I can PRINT both strings and see they're identical. Same operator, same-looking strings, different results. How is this not a bug in Java?

The cruelest part of your situation is the 'sometimes it works' — if `==` failed every time, you'd have fixed this in five minutes. So let's explain both halves: why it fails, and — the half that actually matters — why it ever succeeded.

First half. In Java, a `String` variable doesn't hold the text; it holds a *reference* — an arrow pointing at a String object in memory. So spell out what question `a == b` is actually asking in Java. Is it about the text?

If they're arrows, then `==` compares the arrows — 'do these point at the SAME object?' — not the letters. Two separate String objects could both contain 'go' and `==` would say false because they're two boxes at two addresses. Fine, that explains the user-input failure. But then my test should ALSO have failed! `a` and `b` were two separate variables — why did `==` say true for my two literals?

That's the right question, and its answer is the trap's engine. When the compiler sees the *literal* "go" written twice in your source code, it plays a memory-saving trick called **interning**: identical compile-time literals are folded into ONE shared object in a string pool. So `a` and `b` are two arrows pointing at the same pooled object — `==` honestly answers 'same object? yes.' Your test accidentally asked the one question where arrow-equality and text-equality coincide.

In Python `==` on strings compares contents — always — because Python defines `==` to call the object's own comparison (`__eq__`), and identity has its own separate operator, `is`. So my habit wasn't wrong, it was *Python-shaped*: I assumed `==` means 'equal contents' everywhere. Java splits it differently: `==` is Python's `is`, and for contents I need... `.equals()`, right? So `a.equals(b)` for text, `==` only when I genuinely mean 'the very same object.'

Exactly — and notice you've extracted the transferable lesson, which is bigger than strings: **operators don't have universal meanings; each language assigns them.** When you migrate languages, the danger isn't syntax you don't know — the compiler catches that. It's semantics you *think* you know: things that parse fine, run fine, and mean something different. Interference bugs are fluent-programmer bugs; total beginners never hit this one.

My caching layer has a bug. I added Redis in front of our product database — pages went from 800ms to 40ms, huge win — but now marketing updates a price and customers keep seeing the OLD price for like an hour. Where's the bug in my cache code — some kind of sync flag I forgot?

Read your own description again, slowly: the cache returns what you stored, for as long as you told it to (your TTL is 3600 seconds, I'd bet). It's not malfunctioning — it's keeping the exact promise you wrote. Here's the reframe you need before touching code: a cache is a DEAL. You traded 760ms of latency for something. What did you pay? Name the currency.

I paid... freshness. The 40ms page is fast because it skips the database — which means it can't know the database changed. So 'cache bug' is the wrong frame: staleness isn't a defect, it's the price tag. But then how is caching ever safe? Different data must tolerate different amounts of staleness... product DESCRIPTIONS being an hour old is fine, prices being an hour old costs money and maybe legal trouble.

You just did the analysis most teams skip: a staleness budget per data type. Description: hours are fine. Price: minutes at most, arguably seconds. Stock count: seconds, or customers buy things you don't have. So the design question becomes: for data with a TINY staleness budget, how do you keep cache speed without waiting for the TTL to expire? The update event itself is your resource — marketing SAVED a new price; your system knows the exact moment truth changed. Use it.

Invalidate on write! When the price-update endpoint commits to the database, it also deletes (or overwrites) that product's cache entry — the next reader misses, fetches fresh, repopulates. Staleness window shrinks from an hour to milliseconds. But that couples my update path to the cache... and what about updates that don't go through my endpoint, like the bulk CSV import marketing runs?

And THERE is why cache invalidation is famously one of the two hard problems: every write path must remember to invalidate, forever, including the bulk import someone writes next year. Your defense in layers: (1) invalidate-on-write for the paths you control; (2) a SHORT TTL as the safety net — not an hour but 60 seconds for prices — so any forgotten write path self-heals in a minute instead of never; (3) route writes through one place (a repository layer or DB trigger/change stream) so 'remember to invalidate' lives in one file, not in every developer's head.

Exactly: declaration is a promise, definition is the delivery — and the linker (ld) is the stage that collects deliveries. The compiler turns each .c file into a .o file with IOUs in it: 'I call matrix_multiply, address to be filled in later.' The linker's job is matching every IOU to a definition across all the .o files you hand it. So now diagnose yourself: your compile command is `gcc main.c -o program`. Because the split is a feature you'll be grateful for by your third big project: separate compilation means each .c becomes a .o INDEPENDENTLY — change one file in a million-line project and you recompile one file, then re-link, instead of recompiling the world. It's also how libraries work: printf's definition isn't in any .c you own — it arrives as a precompiled library the linker matches your IOU against.
